To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we identified two genes from the malaria vector Anopheles gambaie that are expressed in response to a meal of human blood and that the promoter regions of these genes drive midgut-specific transgene expression in the mosquito.

we identified two novel midgut-specific promoter regions in Anopheles gambaie and showed that one of these, the G12 promoter, is conserved in Anopheles stepehensi, and that the G12 promoter is a promising tool for the development of Plasmodum-refractory mosquitoes.
we have identified and characterised a novel midgut specific promoter from the Anopheles gmbiae mosquito that is able to drive transgene expression in the mosquito midgut.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the molecular basis of vector competence in Anopheles and with the identification of new targets for the control of malaria.
the study of the Anopheles mosquito, the vector of the malaria parasite, Plasmodium.
the identification of mosquito promoters that can drive the expression of transgenic genes in the midgut of Anopheles mosquitoes, the main vector of the human malarial parasites.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Antryp-1 promoter region is not suitable to drive midgut specific expression in Anopheles species, whereas the G12 promoter is suitable for this task.
both promoters can be used to drive expression in the midgut of Anopheles stepheni, but only the G12 promoter can be used to faithfully mimic the temporal expression pattern.
the G12 promoter can be used for driving transgene expression in Anopheles midgut, and the Antryp-1 promoter is less suitable for this purpose.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
G12 is a useful tool to drive transgene expression at the time when the parasite is in the gut of the mosquito.
the G12 gene is the first midgut-specific gene that can be used as a promoter for transgenic mosquito studies.
we have shown that the G12 promoter is a promising tool for the study of mosquito midgut function and parasite-vector interactions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, while the use of tissue-specific promoters to drive transgene expression in mosquitoes can be successful, the conservation of the regulatory regions between mosquito species is far from complete.
the G12 promoter is highly conserved between A. gambiaes and A. stephensii, and that it may be used in A. stephensis for driving expression in the mosquito midgut.
the Antryp 1 promoter does not appear to be a good choice for driving transgene expression in Anopheles mosquito species.
